place.zh: 沂中医 · 学生健身房 · 国庆
place.en: Yizhong · the student gym · National Day week

setup.zh: 国庆，一个人憋着气卧推，四十公斤的杠落在胸口上。阿禾教他：绷住，推，吐；肉是歇着长的。试训四个，末一名替补，合影里半个人出了框；解剖课上看见那两根白线。
setup.en: National Day week: benching alone, breath held, forty kilos came down on his chest. Ahe teaches him: brace, push, breathe out; muscle grows while it rests. Four reps at tryouts, last substitute in, half out of the team photo; in anatomy he sees the two white threads.

recap.zh: 憋气卧推，杠落在胸口；「绷住，推，吐」「肉是歇着长的」；试训四个，替补第三，末一个进队；解剖课上两根白线，「吐气的时候它说得多一点」。
recap.en: Breath held on the bench, the bar on his chest; "brace, push, breathe out", "muscle grows while it rests"; four reps at tryouts, third substitute, the last one in; two white threads in anatomy, "when you breathe out, it speaks a little more".

en: Forty kilos, down on his chest.
Third substitute, the last one in.

story.zh:
国庆第五天下午，沈芒一个人躺在学生健身房的卧推凳上，憋着一口气，眼前一黑，四十公斤的杠铃落了下来。

黑里头一张小板凳，他太奶坐在上头，老花镜往下一拉，这回没招手，也没说饺子：「芒啊。喘气。」她拿手在膝盖上拍了一下，「你太爷爷推了一辈子磨，一步一口气，也没见他憋着推。」

杠落在胸口上。要是再往上偏一点，就是脖子。

这事，得往回倒五天。

十月一日早上七点半，健身房里一个人也没有。整栋体育馆空荡荡的，玻璃门上贴着「假期开放：七点至二十一点」，前台没人，只有一台饮水机咕嘟咕嘟地响。他躺上卧推凳，握住那根杠——杠是温的。这屋子朝北，不是太阳晒的，是手捂的，一大截，从这头温到那头。大清早，整栋楼没人，这根杠是谁捂热的？

「我的。」镜子那头，马小宝拿毛巾擦着脖子转过身来，「刚推完。一百公斤，五个。」他走过来，低头看着凳子上的沈芒，「你也来？离十七号还有十六天。」

沈芒把阿禾那张通知背给他听：十月十七试训，三项，体能、技术、力量；三项全过进轮换，过两项进替补，过不了两项的，名字从本子上划掉。力量那一项，卧推四十公斤，连推五个。他今天能推多少，他自己知道：空杠二十，两头各加五，三十，推三个。

「差十公斤、两个。小意思。」马小宝下巴一扬，拿鼻孔对着他道，「我高中就是这么练出来的：天天练，练到推不动为止。推的时候憋住气，一口气推上去。漏了气，力就散了。」他拍了拍杠，「来，推。我看着。」

沈芒深吸一口，憋住，推。一个，两个，三个。第三个推上去的时候，脸憋得通红，耳朵里嗡嗡地响。

「好。」马小宝拎起摇杯往外走，走到门口又回头，「十七号，力量那一项，我当保护。我亲手给你数。」

玻璃门在他身后晃了晃。沈芒躺在凳子上喘着气想：他教得这么痛快，是想我过，还是想我不过？想了半天，没想明白。他决定一天练两回。

那张健身卡是中秋夜里办的，一学期三百：两百是回家的车票钱，一百是他妈的过节钱。他跟家里说，国庆学校有集训。这个谎，比上回体测前跟他妈说的那几个都大。

第二天上午他去古籍部。图书馆国庆照开，古籍部只开上午，屋里还是那么冷，还是只有葛奶奶一个。

「奶奶，有没有讲长力气的？《易筋经》那种，天生没力气的人也练得出来的。」

葛奶奶从老花镜上头看他：「易筋经没有。倒有一句硬话，葛洪的书里抄过一句更老的：『[我命在我不在天。]{典=baopu-huangbai}』」

沈芒把这七个字在嘴里过了一遍，像吞了一块热炭。

葛奶奶却又说开了：说她年轻时候插队，生产队里有个大个子，一个人扛两麻袋，后来去了县里的搬运站，一顿吃六个馒头……沈芒听着，心里只剩那七个字。临走取包，她在里头像是还接着说那个搬运站，顺嘴一句：「……扛大包的、打夯的，干重活都喊号子。号子不是唱给人听的，是叫人一使劲，就出气。」

他「哦」了一声。存包的柜子挨着门边那架矮书架，他蹲下去，又从最底层那一函厚书里抽出《九鼎真人手札》的头一册，随手翻到靠前的一页：「十三岁九月，入观。石上测灵，五色俱亮，满殿皆笑。」底下另起一行：「扫地一老者看我一眼：腿稳，心细。」

什么观，什么石头，他不知道；满殿的人笑一个孩子，这个他懂。他把册子塞回去，背上包走了。那七个字他揣走了；号子和手札，他都没往心里去。

国庆七天，六一七只剩他一个。

老蔡回了家，眼镜回了家。第四张空床上本来堆着老蔡的泡面箱，第三天起，上头又摞了两箱，是沈芒的。他算过账：十月的生活费一号到了，先垫走的两百车票钱已经扣在里头，卡又办了，过节钱也花了；剩下的要撑到十一月一号，只够吃泡面。他往每一碗面里加一根火腿肠，觉得这样就算加了肉。

早上一回，下午一回，天天推到推不动。夜里一个人躺在下铺刷卧推的视频，刷到两点。

第四天晚上他妈打来视频。「集训累不累？」「累。」「就你一个？你们宿舍那两个呢？」「……他们不是校队的。」他妈眯着眼往屏幕里瞅：「你手里端的什么？」他把碗往镜头外头挪了挪：「夜宵。食堂饭吃完了。」「钱够不够？」「够。」

挂了视频，他把那半根火腿肠吃了。一个谎，要拿多少个谎去盖？他数了数，今天是第三个。

第五天北风刮了一夜，早上天蓝得发亮。他抱着被子上天台去晒，往西北望，天边横着一道青灰的山脊，一层叠着一层，淡得像拿铅笔描的。宿管阿姨拍着被子道：「蒙山。七十来公里，一年没几回看得见。」他是德州平原上长大的，十八年没见过真山。他说不上那道山脊哪里好，只是看着，看着看着，心里有一块地方静了一静。

下午他给自己加到了四十。推了五天，三十还是三个，一个也没多。他心里发慌：练了五天一点没长，十七号怎么办？命在我——那就是练得还不够狠。四十，推一个也好；推一个，就知道自己够得着。

健身房里没别人。他深吸一口，憋住，把杠从架子上抬下来，放到胸口，往上推。杠走到一半，停住了。他憋着那口气，咬着牙往上顶，脸先红，后紫，脖子上的青筋一根一根暴起来，耳朵里那阵嗡嗡变成了轰轰，眼前一圈一圈地发白，白的边上往里收，收成一条缝——

黑了。

他是叫杠压醒的。四十公斤横在胸口，压得他喘不上来，两只手还攥着杠，攥得指头发白。他不知道自己黑了几秒。想喊，喊不出；想推，推不动。他拿脚蹬着地，把杠一点一点往肚子上滚，滚到大腿根，才坐起来。胸口火辣辣的，一道红印横在那儿。

玻璃门一响，马小宝拎着摇杯进来，看见他，站住了：「……你这是干嘛？」

「我那是在……休息。」

马小宝看了看滚到他腿上的杠，又看了看他胸口的红印，脸上的笑没了。他一只手把杠提回架子上，像放一根晾衣杆：「一个人推？没人保护？憋气是我教的，我没教你一个人憋！」掏出手机，「领队，健身房，新队员自杀！」

沈芒想去抢那个手机，没抢着。

阿禾十分钟就到了，白大褂没脱，马尾辫跑散了。沈芒认识她快一个月，头一回看见她跑。她蹲下来先看他的眼睛，叫他跟着她的指头看左、看右；问他今天几号、这是哪儿；按了按他胸口那道红印，他疼得一缩。

「黑了多久？」

「……不知道。」

「推的时候，憋着气？」

沈芒没说话。马小宝在旁边咳了一声。阿禾站起来看了他一眼，什么也没说。那一眼，马小宝自己往门口去了：「我去楼下买瓶水。」

阿禾从墙角拖过一张垫子，叫他躺平，腿搭上凳子，自己拖了张凳子坐在他头边，拔了笔帽又按上：「憋着气硬推，胸口里的压力一下子顶上去，回心的血过不来，心泵不出去，脑子先断了供。推完一松，血压又猛地往下掉。你今天是在凳子上黑的，杠落在胸口上。落在脖子上，你现在不是坐在这儿听我说话。」

沈芒低着头。

「深吸一口、把肚子绷住，是对的。」她说着，伸出一根指头，冷不防往他肚子上一戳。沈芒「哎」一声，肚子本能地一紧。「就这个。像有人要打你肚子。举重的人都这么干，肚子里的压力把腰撑住，力气才传得出去。可那是一下的事——绷住，推，吐。不是憋着一口气，跟它耗。杠往下放的时候吸，绷住；往上推，过最难那一截，边绷边往外漏，嘴里出声，『嘶——』也行，『呵——』也行，就是别憋死。」

马小宝拎着一瓶水回来，放在垫子边上，没敢走近。阿禾拧开盖子递过去：「喝完。躺够半个钟头。」

沈芒躺在垫子上一口一口喝水。阿禾的手机响了两回，她说「这儿有个人，晚点回」，挂了，低头在本子上记她自己的事。半个钟头，她一回也没看表，到了点，才抬头：「起来。头晕不晕？」

「不晕。」

她把片卸到三十，站在他头顶上，两只手虚托着杠底下。

放下来，吸。肚子鼓起来，绷住。推——「呵——」那口气从牙缝里一点一点吐出去，杠一点一点往上走，眼前没有发白，耳朵里没有轰。一个。放下来，吸；推，呵——两个。三个。四个。第五个推到一半停了一停，他嘴里「呵」得更长了些，杠晃了晃，到底上去了，「咔」地落回架子上。

三十公斤，五个。他推了五天都是三个的那个重量。

他躺在凳子上望着天花板，嘴里还在往外吐那口气，心里头热烘烘的。阿禾没笑，在本子上记了一笔，道：「不是你长了力气。是你前五天推到第三个，就把自己憋黑了。」

沈芒忽然想起葛奶奶在门口那句：扛大包的，一使劲，就出气。原来那句不是废话。她絮叨半天，顺嘴夹的那一句才是有用的——他当时背着包，走了。

她又问了三件事。「几点睡？」「……十二点。」他报了个她表上的数。「练得多勤？」「天天。一天两回。」

阿禾的笔停了：「同一块肉，天天推，它什么时候长？」她拿笔在本子上点了点，「练，是给它下个单子。肉是歇着长的——睡够了，吃够了，它才长。一块肉推完了，隔一两天再推它。」

「那吃什么？」

「鸡蛋，牛奶，肉，豆腐。一顿饭里得有一样。」她抬起头，「你平时吃什么？」

他胸口那道红印还火辣辣地疼。他想起第四张床上摞着的那三箱泡面，想起他妈那句「钱够不够」，想起她本子上他那一行底下要是添上三个字「吃不起」——

「食堂。」

她看了他一会儿，「嗯」了一声，记下了。他看着那支笔落下去，觉得她记下的不是「食堂」两个字，是他这个人。

那天晚上，他烧了一壶开水，拆开一包泡面，加了一根火腿肠。他看着火腿肠在面汤里浮上来，沉下去。他把它捞出来吃了，没尝出味道。

十月七日，老蔡和眼镜回来了。老蔡一进门看见第四张床上那一摞箱子，愣了：「你这是……囤货过冬？」眼镜没笑，拿起一包面翻过来看背面那张表，又摸出手机按了半天：「长肌肉的，一天每公斤体重要一克半上下的蛋白质。你五十九公斤，一天九十克。这一包，十克上下。」他放下面，「你一天得吃九包。」

老蔡道：「九包，那不叫长肌肉，那叫长泡面。」

沈芒没接话。他照阿禾说的，十二点前睡，推一天、歇一天，推的时候吐。

马小宝在健身房撞见他歇着的那天，在跑步机上摇着摇杯：「歇？我教你天天练，她教你隔天练。你听谁的？」

「听不憋气的那个。」

马小宝愣了一下，摇杯停在半空，过了一会儿才道：「行。十七号见。」

此后到试训，阿禾隔一天趁午休来健身房给他保护半个钟头。她站在他头顶上，两只手虚托着杠，一个一个地数，数完了记一笔。他躺在凳子上，看见的是倒过来的她：下巴，马尾辫的尖，和一支一跳一跳的笔。他的力气真的在往上走：三十，五个；三十五，五个；四十，三个，四个。可每天早上捏捏自己的胳膊，还是那根细胳膊。

有一回，他推完了躺着喘气，她忽然问：「你为什么来打球？」

他的心一下子提到了嗓子眼。他盯着天花板上的灯管：「……想跑完一千米。」

「跑完了。」

「那就……想跑快一点。」

阿禾「嗯」了一声，没再问，低头记了一笔。沈芒躺在那儿，觉得自己刚才那口气，憋得比推四十公斤那回还久。

十月十六日，试训前一天，阿禾在器材室给他称：五十八点九公斤。比九月十四那一行，体重少了零点七，体脂多了零点四。

「掉了。」阿禾道。

「力气长了。」

「力气长了，是脑子学会了一齐使劲——头一两个月，长的多半是这个。」阿禾道，「肉，一两没长。」

沈芒捏了捏那根细胳膊：「我天生就这身板。人家天生一米九三。」

她在那一行底下添了一行，抬起头：「天生的定上限；离上限多远，是练的。你离你的上限，远着呢——前提是，得有东西给它长。」她看着他，「你吃的什么，再说一遍。」

器材室的门开着，外头球馆里有人在投篮，砰，砰。

「……食堂。」

阿禾没再问，合上本子：「明天八点。」

那天夜里他睡不着。十二点，一点。上铺的老蔡翻了个身，在黑地里道：「沈忙，睡不着？我教你个法子。」清了清嗓子，「呵——」长长地吐了一口。那是三个礼拜前沈芒教他的。沈芒在黑地里笑了一下，也跟着吐：「呵——」上铺吐一口，下铺吐一口，对床的眼镜在被窝里骂了一句「又吹气球」，翻过身去，过了一会儿，也跟着吐了一口。不知吐到第几口，他睡着了。

十月十七日，星期六，早上八点，体育馆一楼。来试训的二十三个人站成三排。老队员坐在场边看，马小宝坐在最前头，脚边那只大摇杯。

头一项体能，二十米往返跑：跟着录音里的嘀嘀声来回跑，嘀声一回比一回急，跟不上就出局。沈芒慌了一早上，可一跑起来，他的腿认得这个——这一个月，他的二十分钟一天没断过。嘀声越来越急，一个一个的人退了下去，他还在跑，吐，吸，吐。跑到后来两条腿又成了别人借给他的，嗓子眼里又有了那把铁砂；场边马小宝喊了一嗓子：「不行就下来，别吐在地板上！」那一句倒把他喊醒了。他没往嗓子眼里抢气，往外吐，吐干净，又撑了三个来回，撑到嘀声响过去、他的脚还没够着线，才停。二十三个人里，第十四。场边有人「咦」了一声。

第二项技术。运球绕桩上篮，他踢倒了一个桩，上篮没进，补了一个，进了；罚球十个进三个，及格线正是三个，正卡在线上。雷老师在表上打了个钩。

第三项力量。卧推凳摆在场地正中间，四十公斤。马小宝站起来晃到凳子后头，两只手虚托在杠底下，冲他挤了挤眼睛：「来，我给你数。」又俯下身，压低了嗓子，「你黑过一回。今天要是再黑，我可就当着她的面接住你了。」

沈芒躺下去。四周围着二十几个人，场边一排老队员，阿禾坐在记分台后头，本子摊着。他觉得全馆的眼睛都落在他胸口那道还没褪干净的红印上。

放下来，吸。推——「呵——」

「一！」马小宝喊得全馆都听得见。「二！」「三！」

第四个，杠走到一半慢了，慢得像一头拉不动车的老牛。他嘴里「呵」得又长又响，那口气没憋，一丝一丝往外吐，杠一寸一寸往上挪，挪上去了。「……四。」

第五个，杠落到胸口，往上走了一拳，停住了。他吐着气往上顶，顶不动；他没憋——他记着那张小板凳。杠一动不动。马小宝的两只手托上来，把杠接走了，放回架子上。

「四个。差一个。」马小宝冲着全场宣布，又拍了拍杠，「咱们队的吉祥物，尽力了。」

场边的老队员哄地一声笑了，笑声一传，传遍了半个馆。沈芒从凳子上坐起来，坐在那片笑声正中间，脸从耳根烧到脖子。他想起手札里那一条：满殿皆笑。一个孩子，满殿的人。

记分台后头，阿禾没笑。她低头写了一笔，抬起头：「下一个。」笑声停了一停，下一个人站了起来。

中午名单出来了，阿禾站在记分台前头一个一个念。三项全过的四个，进轮换；过两项的三个，进替补。念到替补，她念得跟前头一样，一个字不重：「……替补第三，沈芒。」替补第三，是七个人里的最后一个。往下，她没再念名字。

雷老师把表一合，跟老队员们道：「二十三个里第十四。上个月，一千米倒数第一。三项过两项，按规矩，替补。没什么好笑的。」

马小宝走过来拍他的肩：「恭喜，最后一个。」又压低了嗓子，「过了两项，没过一项——那句话，我先替你留着。」

下午队里照合影。全队二十个人站在篮架底下，前头蹲一排，后头站一排。几个老队员起哄，一声「起——」，把马小宝扛到了肩膀上，他坐在那几只肩膀上，一只手举着摇杯，冲镜头咧着嘴笑。沈芒站在最边上。摄影的同学喊：「最右边那个，往里靠靠！」马小宝在肩膀上头接了一句：「跑龙套的，往里靠！」底下一片笑。他往里挤了挤，挤不进去。

照片发到队群里。他放大了看：马小宝在最上头高高地坐着；他在最右边，半个人出了框，只剩一只胳膊、半张脸、半个笑。他把这半张脸看了很久，到底存了下来——进队的头一张，是他的。

十月二十六日，星期一，下午两点，解剖实验室。白布掀开的还是胸口，这一节看心。

大体老师刘桂芝的心，比他想的小，一只拳头那么大，颜色是暗的。老师拿镊子指着心的上头、顺着脖子下来的两根白线，比鞋带还细：「迷走神经。一边一根，从颅底下来，贴着大血管一路走，走到心，走到肺，走到胃肠。身子里管内脏的神经有两套：一套催，从脊柱两边出来，人一急一怕，它把心催快；一套缓，就是这两根——它一说话，心就慢。」

轮着看。轮到沈芒，他凑近了，那根白线安安静静地贴在血管旁边，什么也不做。他举手：「老师，那怎么叫它说话？」

老师看了他一眼。这孩子每回都问一句书上没有的。「它不归你直接指挥。」她道，「不过它跟着喘气动：吐气的时候，它说得多一点。为什么，下学期生理课讲。」

沈芒「哦」了一声。吐气他会；喘气跟心跳有什么关系，他想不出来，也就没往心里去。
story.en:
On the afternoon of the fifth day of the National Day holiday, Shen Mang lay alone on a bench in the student gym, holding his breath; his sight went black, and the forty-kilo barbell came down.

In the black was a little stool, his great-grandma sitting on it. She pulled her reading glasses down; this time she didn't wave, and she didn't mention dumplings: "Mang. Breathe." She slapped her knee. "Your great-grandpa pushed a millstone his whole life, one step, one breath. Never saw him push holding it in."

The bar landed on his chest. A little higher, and it would have been his neck.

For this, we have to go back five days.

October the first, seven-thirty in the morning, and there was no one in the gym. The whole sports hall was empty; a sign on the glass door said "Holiday hours: 7:00 to 21:00", nobody at the front desk, only a water cooler gurgling. He lay down on the bench and gripped the bar — the bar was warm. The room faced north; it wasn't the sun that had warmed it, it was hands, a long stretch of it, warm from one end to the other. First thing in the morning, nobody in the building — who had warmed this bar?

"Mine." At the far end by the mirror Ma Xiaobao turned round, wiping his neck with a towel. "Just finished. A hundred kilos, five reps." He came over and looked down at Shen Mang on the bench. "You too? Sixteen days to the seventeenth."

Shen Mang recited Ahe's notice to him: tryouts October seventeenth, three tests — fitness, skills, strength; pass all three and you're in the rotation, pass two and you're a reserve, pass fewer than two and your name comes off the book. The strength test was a forty-kilo bench press, five reps in a row. How much he could press today, he knew himself: the empty bar was twenty, five on each end made thirty, three reps.

"Ten kilos and two reps short. Small stuff," said Ma Xiaobao, tipping his chin up to look at him down his nostrils. "That's how I trained in high school: every day, till you can't press any more. When you press, hold your breath and push it up in one go. Let the air out and the power scatters." He patted the bar. "Go on. Press. I'm watching."

Shen Mang took a deep breath, held it, pressed. One, two, three. On the third his face went bright red and his ears rang.

"Good." Ma Xiaobao picked up his shaker and headed out, then turned at the door. "On the seventeenth, strength test, I'll spot you. I'll count them for you myself."

The glass door swung behind him. Shen Mang lay on the bench, panting, and thought: he teaches so readily — does he want me to pass, or want me to fail? He thought about it a long while and couldn't work it out. He decided to train twice a day.

He had bought the gym card on the night of the Mid-Autumn Festival, three hundred for the semester: two hundred was his train fare home, one hundred was his mom's holiday money. He told his family the school had team training over National Day. That lie was bigger than the ones he'd told his mom before the fitness test.

The next morning he went to the rare-books section. The library was open over the holiday, the rare-books room only in the mornings; it was as cold as ever in there, and as ever, only Granny Ge.

"Granny, is there anything about building strength? Something like the *Yijin Jing*, that a person born without strength could still train with?"

Granny Ge looked at him over her reading glasses: "No *Yijin Jing*. But there's one hard saying — Ge Hong copied an older one into his book: 'My fate lies with me, not with Heaven.'"

Shen Mang turned those seven words over in his mouth, like swallowing a hot coal.

But Granny Ge was off again: about being sent down to the countryside when she was young, a big fellow on the production team who could carry two sacks at once, who later went to the county freight depot and ate six steamed buns a meal... Shen Mang listened, and all that was left in his head were the seven words. When he went to collect his bag on the way out, she was still at it inside, as if the freight depot had never ended, and added in passing: "...The sack-carriers, the men driving piles — anyone doing heavy work chanted. The chant isn't sung for anyone to hear. It makes you breathe out the moment you heave."

"Oh," he said. The bag lockers were next to the low bookcase by the door; he crouched down and once again drew the first volume of the *Notes of the Nine Cauldrons Perfected One* out of that case of thick books on the bottom shelf, and opened it at random, somewhere near the front: "Age thirteen, ninth month. Entered the temple. Tested on the stone: all five colours lit, and the whole hall laughed." Below, on a new line: "An old man sweeping the floor gave me one look: legs steady, heart careful."

What temple, what stone, he had no idea; a hall full of people laughing at a child — that he understood. He slid the volume back, shouldered his bag and left. The seven words he took with him; the chant and the journal he didn't take to heart.

For the seven days of National Day, Room 617 had only him.

Old Cai had gone home; Specs had gone home. On the fourth, empty bed Old Cai's instant-noodle boxes were already stacked; from the third day, two more boxes sat on top of them — Shen Mang's. He'd done the sums: October's living money had come in on the first, the two hundred of train fare was already taken out of it, the card was paid for, the holiday money spent; what was left had to last to November the first, and would only buy instant noodles. He added a ham sausage to every bowl and counted that as meat.

One session in the morning, one in the afternoon, every day till he couldn't press any more. At night, alone in the bottom bunk, he scrolled through bench-press videos till two.

On the fourth night his mom called on video. "Is training hard?" "Hard." "Just you? Where are those two from your room?" "...They're not on the team." His mom squinted into the screen: "What's that you're holding?" He moved the bowl out of frame: "Late-night snack. The canteen food was finished." "Have you got enough money?" "Enough."

After the call he ate the other half of the ham sausage. How many lies does it take to cover one lie? He counted: today's was the third.

On the fifth day the north wind had blown all night, and the morning sky was a bright hard blue. He carried his quilt up to the roof to air it, looked northwest, and on the horizon lay a blue-grey ridge, fold on fold, faint as if traced in pencil. The dorm auntie, beating a quilt, said: "Mount Meng. Seventy-odd kilometres. You don't see it many times a year." He had grown up on the Dezhou plain; in eighteen years he had never seen a real mountain. He couldn't have said what was good about that ridge; he just looked, and looking and looking, some place in his heart went still for a moment.

In the afternoon he went up to forty. Five days of pressing, and thirty was still three reps — not one more. Panic rose in him: five days of training and nothing gained — what about the seventeenth? If fate lay with him, then he just hadn't trained hard enough. Forty — even one rep would do; one rep, and he'd know it was within reach.

There was no one else in the gym. He took a deep breath, held it, lifted the bar off the rack, lowered it to his chest, pushed. Halfway up the bar stopped. He held that breath, gritted his teeth, pushed; his face went red, then purple, the veins stood out on his neck one by one, the ringing in his ears turned to a roar, his sight whitened in rings, the white closing in from the edges, narrowing to a slit —

Black.

It was the bar pressing on him that woke him. Forty kilos lay across his chest so he couldn't draw breath; his hands were still clamped on the bar, fingers white. He had no idea how many seconds he'd been out. He tried to shout, and couldn't; tried to push, and couldn't. Pushing with his feet against the floor, he rolled the bar little by little down onto his stomach, down to the tops of his thighs, before he could sit up. His chest burned; a red bar lay across it.

The glass door rattled; Ma Xiaobao came in carrying his shaker, saw him, and stopped. "...What are you doing?"

"I was just... resting."

Ma Xiaobao looked at the bar that had rolled down to his legs, then at the red mark on his chest, and the smile went from his face. With one hand he lifted the bar back onto the rack like a clothes-drying pole: "Pressing alone? No spotter? I taught you to hold your breath, I didn't teach you to hold it on your own!" He pulled out his phone. "Manager. Gym. New player suicide!"

Shen Mang tried to grab the phone, and missed.

Ahe was there in ten minutes, still in her white coat, her ponytail come loose from running. He'd known her almost a month, and it was the first time he'd seen her run. She crouched, looked into his eyes first, had him follow her finger left and right; asked him the date and where he was; pressed the red mark on his chest, and he flinched.

"How long were you out?"

"...Don't know."

"When you pressed — holding your breath?"

Shen Mang said nothing. Ma Xiaobao coughed beside him. Ahe stood up and looked at him once, said nothing. That one look, and Ma Xiaobao took himself off to the door: "I'll go downstairs and buy some water."

Ahe dragged a mat over from the corner, had him lie flat with his legs up on the bench, dragged over a stool and sat by his head, pulled off her pen cap and pushed it back on: "Hold your breath and force it, the pressure in your chest shoots up, the blood coming back to the heart can't get through, the heart can't pump it out, and the brain is the first to lose supply. Then you let go after the press, and your blood pressure drops like a stone. Today you went black on a bench, and the bar landed on your chest. If it had landed on your neck, you wouldn't be sitting here listening to me."

Shen Mang hung his head.

"Deep breath, brace your belly — that part's right." As she spoke she put out one finger and, without warning, jabbed him in the stomach. He went "Ah" and his stomach clenched on its own. "That. As if someone were about to punch you in the gut. Every lifter does it; the pressure inside the belly props up the back, so the force can get through. But that's a one-moment thing — brace, press, breathe out. Not hold one breath and grind it out. On the way down, breathe in and brace; on the way up, through the hardest stretch, keep bracing and let it leak out, make a sound with your mouth — 'ssss' or 'haaa', either one — just don't hold it till you die."

Ma Xiaobao came back with a bottle of water, set it by the mat, and didn't dare come closer. Ahe unscrewed the cap and handed it over: "Finish it. Lie there a full half hour."

Shen Mang lay on the mat drinking the water, sip by sip. Ahe's phone rang twice; she said "There's someone here, I'll be back later", hung up, and bent over her notebook writing her own things. For half an hour she didn't look at her watch once; only when the time was up did she raise her head: "Get up. Dizzy?"

"No."

She took the plates down to thirty and stood over his head, hands hovering under the bar.

Down, breathe in. Belly out, brace. Press — "Haaa —". The breath went out between his teeth a little at a time, and the bar went up a little at a time; no whitening in his eyes, no roar in his ears. One. Down, breathe in; press, haaa — two. Three. Four. The fifth stuck halfway, and he drew the "haaa" out longer; the bar wobbled, and went up after all, and dropped into the rack with a clang.

Thirty kilos, five reps. The weight that had been three reps for five days straight.

He lay on the bench looking at the ceiling, the end of that breath still going out of his mouth, and something warm in his chest. Ahe didn't smile. She wrote a line in her notebook, and said: "You haven't got stronger. For five days you pressed to the third rep and blacked yourself out."

Shen Mang suddenly remembered Granny Ge at the door: the sack-carriers — heave, and the breath goes out. So that line hadn't been idle talk. All that rambling, and the one thing she slipped in on the side was the thing that counted — and he'd shouldered his bag and left.

She asked three more things. "What time do you sleep?" "...Twelve." He gave her the number from her own schedule. "How often do you train?" "Every day. Twice a day."

Ahe's pen stopped. "The same muscle, pressed every day — when does it grow?" She tapped the pen on her notebook. "Training is placing the order. Muscle grows while it rests — enough sleep, enough food, then it grows. Press a muscle, then leave it a day or two before you press it again."

"Then what do I eat?"

"Eggs, milk, meat, tofu. One of those in every meal." She looked up. "What do you usually eat?"

The red mark on his chest still burned. He thought of the three boxes of instant noodles on the empty bed, of his mom's "Have you got enough money", of the words that might go under his line in her notebook — "can't afford food" —

"The canteen."

She looked at him for a while, said "Mm", and wrote it down. He watched the pen come down and felt that what she had written wasn't the word "canteen" — it was him.

That night he boiled a kettle, opened a packet of noodles, added a ham sausage. He watched the sausage float up in the broth and sink again. He fished it out and ate it, and didn't taste a thing.

On October the seventh Old Cai and Specs came back. Old Cai walked in, saw the stack of boxes on the fourth bed, and stopped: "What's this... stocking up for winter?" Specs didn't laugh. He picked up a packet of noodles, turned it over to the table on the back, took out his phone and tapped for a while: "To build muscle you need about a gram and a half of protein per kilo of body weight a day. You're fifty-nine kilos; that's ninety grams a day. This packet's about ten." He put it down. "You'd need nine packets a day."

Old Cai said: "Nine packets — that's not building muscle, that's building noodles."

Shen Mang said nothing. He did what Ahe had said: in bed before twelve, press one day, rest the next, breathe out on the press.

The day Ma Xiaobao caught him resting at the gym, he was on the treadmill shaking his shaker: "Resting? I tell you every day, she tells you every other day. Who are you listening to?"

"The one who doesn't hold their breath."

Ma Xiaobao paused, the shaker stopped in mid-air, and after a moment he said: "Fine. See you on the seventeenth."

From then until tryouts, Ahe came to the gym every other day in her lunch break and spotted him for half an hour. She stood over his head, hands hovering under the bar, counting one by one, and wrote a line when she'd finished. What he saw from the bench was her upside down: a chin, the tip of a ponytail, and a pen that jumped with every rep. His strength really was climbing: thirty, five; thirty-five, five; forty, three, four. But every morning he pinched his arm, and it was still the same thin arm.

Once, when he'd finished and lay there panting, she suddenly asked: "Why did you come to play ball?"

His heart leapt into his throat. He stared at the tube light on the ceiling: "...I wanted to finish a thousand metres."

"You finished it."

"Then... I want to run a bit faster."

Ahe said "Mm", didn't ask further, and bent to write a line. Shen Mang lay there feeling he had held that breath longer than the one under forty kilos.

October the sixteenth, the day before tryouts, Ahe weighed him in the equipment room: fifty-eight point nine kilos. Against the line from September the fourteenth, weight down by point seven, body fat up by point four.

"Down," said Ahe.

"I'm stronger."

"Stronger means your brain has learned to make everything push together — the first month or two, that's mostly what you gain," said Ahe. "Muscle, you haven't put on an ounce."

Shen Mang pinched the thin arm: "I was born with this build. Other people are born six foot four."

She added a line under that row and looked up: "What you're born with sets the ceiling; how far you are from it is training. You're a long way from your ceiling — provided there's something for it to grow on." She looked at him. "What do you eat? Tell me again."

The equipment-room door stood open; out in the gym someone was shooting. Thump. Thump.

"...The canteen."

Ahe didn't ask again. She closed the notebook: "Tomorrow, eight o'clock."

That night he couldn't sleep. Twelve. One. In the top bunk Old Cai rolled over and said into the dark: "Shen Mang-the-busy, can't sleep? I'll teach you a trick." He cleared his throat — "Haaa —" — one long breath out. That was what Shen Mang had taught him three weeks before. Shen Mang laughed once in the dark, and breathed out too: "Haaa —" Top bunk, one breath; bottom bunk, one breath; Specs in the opposite bed swore "Balloons again" into his quilt and turned over, and after a while, he breathed out too. Somewhere around the who-knows-what breath, he fell asleep.

October the seventeenth, Saturday, eight in the morning, the ground floor of the sports hall. The twenty-three trying out stood in three rows. The old hands sat courtside to watch, Ma Xiaobao at the very front, the big shaker at his feet.

First, fitness: the twenty-metre shuttle run — back and forth to the beeps on the recording, each beep sooner than the last; fall behind and you're out. Shen Mang had been in a panic all morning, but once he was running, his legs knew this — in a month, his twenty minutes hadn't missed a day. The beeps came faster and faster, one person after another dropped out, and he was still running: out, in, out. Later his legs were someone else's again and the hot grit was back in his throat; from the sideline Ma Xiaobao yelled, "Quit if you can't, just don't puke on the floor!" — and that woke him up. He didn't snatch at air in his throat; he breathed out, emptied it, and held on for three more lengths, until the beep had sounded and his foot still hadn't reached the line. Fourteenth of twenty-three. Someone on the sideline went "Huh."

Second, skills. Dribbling round the cones to a lay-up, he kicked a cone over, missed the lay-up, put the rebound back in; free throws, three of ten, and three was the passing line — right on it. Coach Lei ticked the sheet.

Third, strength. The bench was set in the middle of the court, forty kilos. Ma Xiaobao got up, ambled round behind the bench, hands hovering under the bar, and winked at him: "Come on, I'll count." Then he bent down and dropped his voice: "You've blacked out once. Black out again today and I'll be catching you in front of her."

Shen Mang lay down. Twenty-odd people stood around him, a row of old hands courtside, Ahe behind the scorers' table with her notebook open. He felt every eye in the hall on the red mark across his chest that hadn't yet faded.

Down, breathe in. Press — "Haaa —"

"One!" Ma Xiaobao shouted so the whole hall could hear. "Two!" "Three!"

On the fourth, the bar slowed halfway, slow as an old ox that can't pull the cart. His "haaa" came long and loud; he didn't hold the breath, he let it out thread by thread, and the bar crept up inch by inch, and made it. "...Four."

On the fifth, the bar came down to his chest, went up a fist's width, and stopped. He pushed, breathing out, and it wouldn't go; he didn't hold his breath — he remembered the little stool. The bar didn't move. Ma Xiaobao's hands came up under it, took it away, and set it on the rack.

"Four. One short." Ma Xiaobao announced it to the whole hall, then patted the bar. "Our team mascot. He gave it his all."

The old hands on the sideline burst out laughing, and the laughter spread until half the hall was laughing. Shen Mang sat up on the bench, sitting in the middle of that laughter, his face burning from his ears to his neck. He thought of the entry in the journal: the whole hall laughed. One child, a whole hall.

Behind the scorers' table, Ahe didn't laugh. She bent her head, wrote a line, and looked up: "Next." The laughter paused, and the next person stood up.

At noon the list came out, and Ahe stood in front of the scorers' table and read it name by name. The four who had passed all three went into the rotation; the three who had passed two went to the reserves. When she reached the reserves she read them the same way as the rest, not one word heavier: "...Third reserve, Shen Mang." Third reserve was the last of the seven. Below that, she read no more names.

Coach Lei snapped his sheet shut and said to the old hands: "Fourteenth of twenty-three. Last month, dead last in the thousand metres. Two of three, by the rules, reserve. Nothing funny about it."

Ma Xiaobao came over and patted his shoulder: "Congratulations. Last one in." Then, voice low: "Passed two, failed one — that thing I'm going to say for you, I'll hang on to it for now."

In the afternoon the team took its photo. All twenty of them under the basket, a row crouching in front, a row standing behind. A few of the old hands whooped, "Up —", and hoisted Ma Xiaobao onto their shoulders; he sat up there on those shoulders, one hand holding up his shaker, grinning at the camera. Shen Mang stood at the very edge. The student taking the picture called: "Far right — move in! Move in more!" From up on the shoulders Ma Xiaobao added: "Bit-part player, move in!" Laughter below. He squeezed in, and couldn't get in.

The photo went to the team group. He zoomed in: Ma Xiaobao up top, sitting high; himself at the far right, half out of the frame — one arm, half a face, half a smile. He looked at that half face a long time, and saved it after all. The first picture since he made the team, and it was his.

October the twenty-sixth, Monday, two in the afternoon, the anatomy lab. The white cloth was folded back from the chest again; this session was the heart.

The heart of their silent teacher, Liu Guizhi, was smaller than he'd imagined, the size of a fist, dark in colour. The instructor's forceps pointed to two white threads coming down the neck above the heart, thinner than a shoelace: "The vagus nerve. One each side, down from the base of the skull, running alongside the great vessels, to the heart, to the lungs, to the stomach and bowel. The nerves that run the organs come in two sets: one that drives — out from either side of the spine; when you're pressed or frightened, it drives the heart faster — and one that slows, which is these two. When it speaks, the heart slows."

They took turns to look. When it was Shen Mang's turn he leaned in close; the white thread lay quietly beside the vessel, doing nothing at all. He raised his hand: "Teacher, how do you make it speak?"

The instructor looked at him. This boy always had one question that wasn't in the book. "It doesn't take orders from you directly," she said. "But it moves with your breathing: when you breathe out, it speaks a little more. Why — physiology, next semester."

"Oh," said Shen Mang. Breathing out he could do; what breathing had to do with a heartbeat he couldn't imagine, so he didn't take it to heart.
